newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures surged a point on Monday on a combination of hopes for French rate cuts, expectations of demand from domestic investors and short covering by investors who sold on Friday.

Traders said while the French market had managed to decouple somewhat from the U.S. bond market, fears of declines in the Treasury, especially with a key consumer price report due on Tuesday, held French bonds back later in the session.
They said the market got its initial boost from a number of non-resident funds buying back contracts they had sold after the strong U.S. jobs report on Friday.
"The volume was concentrated at the long end where a couple of funds went through the pain barrier and got out," a futures trader at a French bank said.

"Right now the move is justified," he said. "There's no sign either of the two major continental economies are getting any better, which means there's a limit to how far long yields can rise, and even if the (U.S. Federal Reserve) hikes it's not a cycle that's going to be exported to Europe."
Traders said the turnaround in the market had made a test of the 130.20 contract high hit on December 3 a real possibility. The contract peaked at 129.84 on Monday.
Once again PIBOR contracts rallied on hopes for interest rate cuts in France as soon as Thursday when the Bank of France monetary policy council meets.

A Reuter poll of economists showed nine out of 15 expected the central bank to trim the intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, five basis points to 3.10 percent this week.
The March PIBOR contract set an all-time high at 96.82 and has now climbed steadily for six consecutive sessions. The June contract outperformed March, also setting a new high at 96.86.
The gap between implied French and German three-month rates also narrowed. Futures implied the gap would be eight basis points by the end of March, four at the end of June and zero by September.
Some analysts said the moves at the front of the curve had now priced most of the potential good news on rates, without a further cut in rates from the Bundesbank.

Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said yields on short-dated government bonds, or BTANs, were being dragged down by the PIBOR rally, forcing investors to move further along the curve to the five-year zone.
They're starting to put money to work at five-years rather than two. It's a classic flattening in a long end bull market," he said. "There are not many reasons to be holding onto paper in two years."
The main focus in the cash market on Monday was the sale of five billion francs of a 5.5 percent 2004 bond issued by Austria at seven basis points over equivalent French government bonds.
Traders said the bond attracted good interest from investors and that the spread was put at seven, rather than the expected six basis points, because of the sharp rally in bond prices on Monday.

Analysts said one of the attractions of the Austrian bonds was the promise of liquidity in years to come as the bonds will be come fungible with an existing schilling Bund in the event of France and Austria joining monetary union.

The 10-year spread between French and German government bond yields, using the 6.50 percent 2006 OAT, moved to minus 11 basis points from minus seven on Friday while the two-year spread moved to parity.
Call money remained unchanged at 3-3/16 5/16 percent.
